'''Peter Duncumb''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|FRS|FInstP}} (born 26 January 1931) is a British physicist specialising in [[X-ray microscopy]] and [[microanalysis]].<ref name="FRS" /> He is best known for his contribution to the development of the first [[electron microprobe]].<ref name="FRS" /><ref name="Electron Probe Quantitation 1991 p. ">{{cite book | editor-last=Heinrich | editor-first=K. F. J. | editor-last2=Newbury | editor-first2=Dale E. | title=Electron Probe Quantitation | publisher=Springer US | publication-place=Boston, MA | year=1991 | isbn=978-1-4899-2619-7 | doi=10.1007/978-1-4899-2617-3 | s2cid=32240607 }}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Duncumb was educated at [[Clare College, Cambridge]]. He earned his PhD in 1957, under the supervision of [[Vernon Ellis Cosslett]].<ref name="whoswho" /><ref name="Melford 2004 pp. 289–308">{{cite book | last=Melford | first=D.A. | title=Advances in Imaging and Electron Physics | chapter=3.4 Tube Investments Research Laboratories and the Scanning Electron Probe Microanalyser | publisher=Elsevier | year=2004 | volume=133 | isbn=978-0-12-014775-5 | issn=1076-5670 | doi=10.1016/s1076-5670(04)33025-9 | pages=289–308}}</ref>

== Career ==
Duncumb worked at the [[University of Cambridge]] as a [[research fellow]] from 1957 until 1959.<ref name="whoswho" /> He carried out key work on the development of the [[Electron microprobe|scanning electron probe X-ray microanalyser]], now a common tool for surface studies in most materials laboratories.<ref name="FRS" /><ref name="Cosslett 2004 pp. 237–250">{{cite book | last=Cosslett | first=V.E. | title=Advances in Imaging and Electron Physics | chapter=3.1 The Development of the X-ray Projection Microscope and the X-ray Microprobe Analyser at the Cavendish Laboratory | publisher=Elsevier | year=2004 | volume=133 | isbn=978-0-12-014775-5 | issn=1076-5670 | doi=10.1016/s1076-5670(04)33019-3 | pages=237–250}}</ref> His early work led to the first commercial instrument for imaging the distribution of selected chemical elements on a microscale, providing essential information for [[failure analysis]] and the [[Materials science|development of new materials]].<ref name="FRS" />

After joining the Central Laboratories of [[TI Group|Tube Investments]] in 1959, he built a second instrument, known as EMMA, combining X-ray microanalysis with [[transmission electron microscopy]]. This made possible a finer analysis of [[thin film]] and [[Particulates|particulate]] samples, and led again to commercial production. Later, he took on broader management responsibilities, retiring in 1987 after 8 years as Laboratory Director.<ref name="FRS" />

Since 1988, he has been working as a consultant on the interpretation of [[X-ray spectroscopy|X-ray spectra]], and on the use of [[phased array]]s in [[ultrasonic testing]]. He also served as chairman of the [[Royal Society]]'s Paul Instrument Fund. He is an honorary member of both the US and European [[microbeam]] analysis societies.<ref name="FRS" />

== Awards and honours ==
In 1966, Duncumb won the Charles Vernon Boys Prize (now known as the Moseley Medal) of the [[Institute of Physics]] for "the design and construction of the scanning electron probe system for localized [[elemental analysis]]".<ref name="IOP Publishing 1966 pp. 37–38">{{cite journal | title=Announcements | journal=Physics Bulletin | publisher=IOP Publishing | volume=17 | issue=2 | year=1966 | issn=0031-9112 | doi=10.1088/0031-9112/17/2/001 | pages=37–38}}</ref> He was elected a [[List of Fellows of the Royal Society elected in 1977|Fellow of the Royal Society (FRS) in 1977]].<ref
